links.note: Severus of Antioch wrote to Egyptian clergy after his exile began. He told them he cared even more for Alexandria's church than for Antioch's. He says groups long cut off from the Egyptian church joined it through his work. Dioscorus II, patriarch of Alexandria, took his advice, he writes.

links.note: John of Ephesus says Justinian sent envoys with gold and baptismal robes to the Nobadae, asking them to join his church. The king accepted the gifts but refused the emperor's faith, and sent a written answer. John wrote for the rival party, and his is the only account of this exchange.

links.note: Justinian confirmed the anathema that the sees of the patriarchs and the monks had passed on Severus of Antioch. His law said Severus's books must be burned, and it kept him out of the capital. Evagrius says it also threatened those who held to his views with the highest penalties.

links.from_name: The Church of the East under Persia
links.note: In 612 the Persian king had the bishops of the Church of the East debate the Miaphysites at his court. A statement drawn up for that meeting says Christ has two natures. It charges Severus and his disciples with leaving the foundation of the faith by teaching one.

sources.work: Synodicon Orientale, Appendix III: documents of the bishops' assembly of 612 (trans. Chabot, 1902)
sources.quote: mais ce sont Sévère et ses disciples qui s’en sont écartés, eux qui professent que le Christ est une seule nature et une seule personne.

sources.work: J.-B. Chabot, Synodicon Orientale (Paris, 1902), introduction to Appendix III, on the assembly of 612 called by Khosrow at Gabriel of Singar's urging for a public debate with the Monophysites (vendored edition, file lines 37347-37356)

links.from_name: The Church of the East under Persia
links.note: Cosmas, an Alexandrian traveler writing around 550, reported a church on India's pepper coast and a bishop at Kalyan appointed from Persia. He does not say the pepper-coast church was under Persia. No source from his time ties it to the Kerala church of the 800s, so the evidence is slight.

sources.work: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography III (trans. McCrindle, 1897)

links.note: Evagrius says the patriarch of Jerusalem sent leading monks from Judea to Constantinople. This was before the council of 553. Conon was from the monastery of Saba, and Rufus was from that of Theodosius. At court it was they who raised the questions about what Origen taught.

sources.work: Evagrius Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History IV.38 (Walford, 1846)

links.note: In 554 a council met at Dvin under the catholicos Nerses II. It confirmed that the Armenian church said no to the Council of Chalcedon. Against the claims of that council, it proclaimed the faith of Ephesus. This rests on modern histories of that church, and most of all on the one by Malachia Ormanian.

sources.work: Malachia Ormanian, The Church of Armenia (trans. G. Marcar Gregory, 1912), pp. 35-36 (the synods of Douine, 506 and 554) and p. 40 (Nerses II at Douine, 554) (vendored: cic/texts/ormanian_church-of-armenia_gregory1912.txt)

links.note: The Armenian historian Malachia Ormanian tells of a council in Dvin in 506. He says bishops from Georgia, Armenia and Albania all met there. A Syriac chronicle of about 555 says the Christian peoples of the north had one catholicos, at Dvin. It then calls Georgia a land with a Christian prince, subject to Persia.

links.note: Elias led the church of Armenia as its catholicos from 703 to 717. He worked to keep Albania in the Armenian communion. sources.work: Sebeos, History (Histoire d'Héraclius), ch. XXXIII (French trans. Macler, 1904)

links.note: In 802 Charlemagne gathered abbots and monks at Aachen. There they read the Rule of Saint Benedict together. He then ordered that anything done in monasteries against the rule be put right by it. Sixty years before, in 742, Carloman's council had told monks and nuns to live by the same rule.

sources.work: Lorsch Annals for 802, as printed in the headnote to the Aachen synod of 802 (MGH Capitularia regum Francorum I)
sources.locus: Ann. Lauresh. a. 802 (Capit. I, no. 36-41, headnote)
sources.quote: Similiter in ipso synodo congregavit universos abbates et monachos qui ibi aderant, et ipsi inter se conventum faciebant et legerunt regulam sancti patris Benedicti, et eam tradiderunt sapientes in conspectu abbatum et monachorum.

sources.work: Karlmann's capitulary of 742 (Concilium Germanicum), c. 7 (MGH Capitularia regum Francorum I)
sources.quote: Et ut monachi et ancillae Dei monasteriales iuxta regulam sancti Benedicti ordinare et vivere, vitanii propriam gubernare studeant

sources.work: Francis Aidan Gasquet, introduction to The Rule of Saint Benedict (Chatto and Windus edition, 1925)

links.note: Two Benedictine editors of the Rule draw on the later customs of Cluny to explain how it was lived. They are Oswald Hunter Blair, in 1907, and Cardinal Gasquet. Gasquet calls it practically the only rule for monks in the West from the ninth to the twelfth century. The case rests on these two editors, not on Cluny's own texts.

sources.work: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, explanatory notes to The Rule of St. Benedict (Sands, 1907)
Francis Aidan Gasquet, introduction to The Rule of Saint Benedict (Chatto and Windus edition, 1925)

links.to_name: The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great
links.note: Before he was pope, Gregory lived at Constantinople as the pope's envoy. In his Morals on Job, he recalls a debate on the resurrection with Eutychius, the city's bishop. It went on until Emperor Tiberius heard them both. Paul the Deacon tells the same story in the late 700s.

sources.quote: In his days while the blessed Gregory, the deacon who afterwards became Pope, was papal delegate at the same imperial city, he composed books of Morals

links.to_name: The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great
links.note: Gregory wrote often to Gaul. He answered Queen Brunhild's letters, and warned four leading bishops that holy orders there were being bought. Gregory of Tours recorded the pope's election in 590, as his own deacon reported it on his return from Rome.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Register VI.50, To Queen Brunichild (NPNF 2.12, Barmby)
sources.quote: The tenor of your letters, which evinces a religious spirit and the earnestness of a pious mind, causes us not only to commend the purpose of your request, but also to grant willingly what you demand.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Register IX.106, To Syagrius, Aetherius, Virgilius and Desiderius (NPNF 2.13, Barmby)
sources.quote: I apprize you to wit, that we have long heard it currently reported how that in the regions of Gaul sacred orders are conferred through simoniacal heresy.

sources.work: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks X.1 (Dalton 1927)
sources.quote: And because the Church of God could not remain without a leader, the whole people chose the deacon Gregory.

links.to_name: The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great
links.note: Gregory first met Leander of Seville at Constantinople, and the two kept writing to each other. In one letter Gregory said that Leander's letters had made him love King Reccared. Later he wrote to the king himself. He praised the conversion of the whole Gothic nation.

links.to_name: The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great
links.note: Gregory wrote to all the bishops of Numidia, answering a request they had sent to his predecessor. He let them keep their old customs for choosing a senior bishop. But he barred bishops who had come over from the Donatists from that rank.

links.note: Belisarius took Carthage in 533. The Arian priests fled, and the orthodox took back the shrine of Cyprian. Then, Procopius says, Justinian let no Christian outside the orthodox faith be baptized or share in any other sacrament. So Arian soldiers could not baptize their children.

sources.work: Procopius, History of the Wars III.21, the Vandalic War (Dewing 1916)
sources.quote: And the priests of the Arians were off in flight, while the Christians who conform to the orthodox faith came to the temple of Cyprian,

sources.work: Procopius, History of the Wars IV.14, the Vandalic War (Dewing 1916)
sources.quote: For the Emperor Justinian did not allow any Christian who did not espouse the orthodox faith to receive baptism or any other sacrament.

links.note: Writing around 640, Jonas of Bobbio tells how Columbanus sailed from Ireland and set up Luxeuil in Gaul. Local nobles then set up houses for monks under his rule. Among them were Donatus, bishop of Besançon, and Dado at Rebais. His book of penances, which he wrote on the Continent, set the model for later Frankish ones.

sources.work: Jonas of Bobbio, Life of St. Columban 10, tr. Munro 1895
sources.quote: So they embarked, and began the dangerous journey across the channel and sailed quickly with a smooth sea and favorable wind to the coast of Brittany.

links.to_name: The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great
links.note: Around 600 the Irish monk Columbanus wrote from Luxeuil to Pope Gregory. He stood up for the Irish date of Easter and asked why Gregory kept a dark Easter. Irish scholars, he said, had never taken up the Easter tables of Victorius. No reply from Gregory survives.

sources.work: Columbanus, Letter to Pope Gregory (Gregory, Register, Ep. IX.127 in Barmby's numbering), NPNF II.13
sources.quote: Why then dost thou, who art so wise, the brilliant lights indeed of whose sacred genius are diffused, as in ancient times, through the world,—why dost thou keep a dark Easter?

sources.work: Columbanus, Letter to Pope Gregory, NPNF II.13
sources.quote: For know thou that by our masters and the Irish ancients, who were philosophers and most wise computists in constructing calculations, Victorius was not received, but held rather worthy of ridicule or of excuse than as carrying authority.

sources.work: James Barmby, note to Columbanus's letter to Gregory, NPNF II.13 (1898)

links.note: Bede, writing in the eighth century, says Columba's successors still held the island of Iona. In 1938 George MacLeod founded the Iona Community there and set about rebuilding its abbey. No source shows what it drew from Columba's monks, so this rests on place alone.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), III.4
sources.quote: whereupon he also received of them the aforesaid island for a monastery, for it is not very large, but contains about five families, according to the English computation. His successors hold the island to this day

sources.work: Ron Ferguson, Chasing the Wild Goose: The Story of the Iona Community (1988)

links.note: Around 600 the Irish monk Columbanus wrote a letter to Pope Gregory. In it he cited Gildas, the British monk and writer. He said that a writer named Vennianus had asked Gildas about monks who left their monastery. Gildas, he said, had given him a most elegant reply.

sources.work: Columbanus, Letter to Pope Gregory, NPNF II.13
sources.quote: The author Vennianus enquired about these of Giltas, who replied to him most elegantly

sources.work: Columbanus, Letter to Pope Gregory, NPNF II.13
sources.quote: those monks who for a closer sight of God, or inflamed by a longing for a more perfect life, going against their vows, leave the places of their first conversion

links.note: Bede tells of two meetings around 603 between Augustine of Canterbury and the British bishops. The first was at Augustine's Oak. Pope Gregory had put the British bishops under Augustine, but at the second meeting they would not take him as their archbishop. Bede wrote this more than a century later.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), II.2, chapter title

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), II.2

links.note: Laurentius, who followed Augustine, wrote to the British clergy and urged them into Catholic unity. Later, Bede reports, Aldhelm wrote a book against the way they fixed the date of Easter. Bede himself complained about the Britons. They would not share the faith with the English, he said, yet still held to their errors.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), II.4
sources.quote: The same Laurentlus and his fellow bishops wrote a letter to the priests of the Britons, suitable to his rank, by which he endeavoured to confirm them in Catholic unity

links.note: In his history of the English church, Bede cites Gildas as the Britons' own historian for their sins after the Romans left. Bede then adds a charge of his own: that the Britons never preached the faith to the English.

links.note: At the third council of Toledo in 589, the Gothic bishops condemned the faith they had held, which the council called Arian. They cursed anyone who still kept the communion that came from Arius. They also cursed the booklet issued in King Leovigild's reign to bring Romans over to it. Eight bishops, Ugnas and Murila among them, signed as men entering the catholic church.

sources.work: Third Council of Toledo (589), anathema 1, Collectio canonum Ecclesiae Hispanae (Madrid, 1808)

links.note: At Whitby in 664, Bede says, the English priest Wilfrid argued against the Easter kept by Bishop Colman and his Irish clergy. He said Rome, Italy, Gaul, Africa, Asia and Egypt kept the Roman date, and he called the other side obstinate. King Oswy then chose to follow Peter, who held the keys of heaven.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation III.25 (Giles/Jane 1903)

links.note: The monks of Cîteaux set out to keep the Rule of St Benedict more plainly. No early Cistercian text quoted here says so in their own words. A 1907 editor of the Rule notes only that early Cistercian statutes, like the Rule, set times when monks might talk.

links.note: Michael the Syrian, patriarch from 1166, built his world chronicle partly from older Syriac histories. At one point he marks where the chronicles of John of Asia and Zacharias the Rhetor take over as his sources. Elsewhere he quotes John speaking in his own voice about a dispute at the emperor's court.

sources.work: Michael the Syrian, Chronicle, Book VIII (French trans. Chabot)
